hints: Look at the central $-$ symbol and check whether each arrowhead points toward it or away from it in diagrams A and B.
Recall that electric field direction is defined as the force on a small positive test charge, so a negative source charge must attract it.
Compare radial straight lines that meet the charge with the concentric circles in C and D, and ask which shape shows attraction straight toward a point.
walkthrough: Identify the source: a single isolated negative point charge marked $-$ at the centre, so the pattern must be symmetric in all directions.
State the direction rule: field direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge, given by $F = qE$.
Since $q$ is positive for the test charge and the source is negative, the Coulomb force is attractive, so every field line must point radially inward toward the $-$ charge.

Reject circular patterns: diagrams C and D show closed concentric loops tangential to the charge, which never point toward or away from the centre, so they cannot be an electrostatic point-charge field.
Check diagram A: it mixes inward and outward arrows, with vertical and horizontal arrows pointing away from the charge, so it does not show uniform attraction.
Check diagram B: all eight straight lines are radial and every arrowhead points directly inward to the $-$ charge with radial symmetry. This is option B.

options.A: Some arrows point away from the central $-$ charge, which would represent repulsion of a positive test charge and is correct for a positive charge, not a negative charge.
options.B: All lines are radial, symmetric and point directly toward the central $-$ charge, showing attraction of a positive test charge.
options.C: Concentric circular loops are not radial and do not start or end on the point charge, so they cannot represent the electrostatic field of an isolated charge.
options.D: Concentric circular loops in the opposite sense are still tangential, not radial toward the charge, so they cannot represent the field of an isolated point charge.
